utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I was told, it's full house. Yes. Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-O1-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would both parties make their appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Sureta Chana, Philip Weiner, Manoj Sachdeva for the Prosecution, very ably assisted by Ana Vrljic as our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Morrissey is my name and I appear for Mr. Halilovic with Mr. Mettraux and with Mr. Cengic as legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morissey. This must be the first Status Conference for the Tribunal for this year. This is likely to be the last Status Conference before the Trial Chamber of this Trial Chamber. Being the ninth one, I guess. And this is -- this case is due -- the trial of this case is due to start very soon, i.e., on Monday, 24th of this month, less than two weeks' time from now. However, there are a number of outstanding motions which I'm going through briefly with the parties. I think the most urgent matter would be the Prosecution's request for certification for interlocutory appeal against our decision on motion to amend the indictment. The Chamber is actively reviewing the motion, and I would say that the decision will be issued very soon. Second motion. Let me deal with the minor one. The most recent one filed by the Prosecution, which is an application for leave to disclose Rule 66(A)(ii) material, filed on 10th of January. It seems to be a witness statement of the existing witnesses given to a local Bosnian authority, some 11 years ago or 12 years ago. I wonder if there's anything to say to this from the Defence on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we don't oppose it, Your Honour. We are troubled by the length of time and the nearness to the trial but that is the only comment we can make at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I like to grant it orally. Hereby that motion is granted. Next motion I'd like to raise is the motion to vary the number of 65 witnesses -- 65 ter witnesses. And it has not been decided yet whether this Trial Chamber will issue a decision on this or the matter will be transferred, deferred to the actual Trial Chamber hearing the case. But there are a couple of things to explore on part of myself. Is it correct -- am I correct in understanding that the old statements of those witnesses to be added are actually disclosed, be it under 66(A)(ii) regime or 66(B) or 67?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Can we indicate that at least with respect to the witnesses Ramiz Delalic and Enver Mujezinovic, we don't think all of the statements have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Could you give me the second name of the second witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. M-u-j-e-z-i-n-o-v-i-c, Enver Mujezinovic. Your Honour, I could indicate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Pardon me. Have I misspelled again? Mujezinovic. It's correct. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Delalic, all the statements were disclosed except for the transcript of the suspect interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty is with Mr. Delalic, we have here the suspect interview and in the text of that is disclosed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again. You were given the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We have been given the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which has been outstanding --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for quite a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We have that and we have it -- we've now endeavoured to read as much as we can of it. However, within the text of it, it discloses two matters of interest. Firstly, a 1996 interview which we do not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 1996 interview. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That interview we understand was an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. There is also referred to what the witness claims to be 50 contacts with a particular investigator, named Mihailov. We do not have any records of those contacts. Mr. Mujezinovic mentions that it is the third statement that he has made. We've been provided with two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the one related to the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What we referred to, obviously, as an earlier one. Sorry, Your Honour, does that deal with the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 1996 -- interview in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean that you have the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So both the tape and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the context with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, we don't know who the original -- the two are separate. The 1996 interview was, we believe, with an investigator, but we don't know who that was. However, the witness mentions numerous contacts, he says 50, with the investigator Mihailov. They're quite separate matters. We would like to have the 1996 tape and transcript, and we would like to have such material that there is arising from the 50 contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can I take it, as you are saying, that the Prosecution is duty-bound to keep records of every contact with the suspect or potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It would be our position that they're bound to keep records, and it would be our position -- in fact, elsewhere, we argue that they are indeed duty-bound to provide and to preserve the records of the questions that they've asked. But at the least, we say they should preserve records of contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. If I can hear from the Prosecution on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In respect of Delalic and the -- we have handed over now the transcript yesterday, and what my learned friend is referring to is within the transcript Mr. Delalic obviously talks about interviews with Mr. Mihailov, but we have no statements that we have -- that those contacts generated. We have handed over everything that we have in our custody over to the Defence. There is no other material which is still pending to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that the final position or there's room to -- for a more investigation on that matter, whether you have any records of interview or meeting with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In respect of Delalic, Your Honour, I think that is the Prosecution's final position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Since Mr. Delalic is mentioned, I have a feeling that we are required to make a ruling on a sort of hypothetical Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond motion, which means that I was told, informed by the Senior Legal Officer, that OTP has not yet decided whether to call Mr. Delalic or not. Is it still the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: As I mentioned at the 65 ter conference, Your Honour, that we were all awaiting the transcript, the Defence and the Prosecution, and now that we've just got the transcript, the Prosecution team is going to look at the transcript and make the final decision, and we shall be able to advise the Chamber and the Defence within the next two days whether we will be -- whether we still want Delalic on our witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're suggesting that you can make the decision in two days?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the end of -- today is Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've just been advised by my co-counsel here, Friday. Would that be all right? Because one of our prosecuting counsel is not returning until Thursday, I've just been reminded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would be grateful that decision can be made by the end of Thursday, and let the Chamber know about the result of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about the -- I'm sorry about the pronunciation -- Mujezinovic, the second witness. Third witness statement of his?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We have disclosed, as far as we are concerned, all the statements of Witness Mujezinovic, but we will look into this matter. We'll ask our case manager, Ana, to see and do some more investigations to see if there is another witness statement. Sometimes witnesses do make mistakes as to how many witnesses -- how many statements they've given, but of course if there is another one, we will look into it. But as of now, we don't know of any other statement other than the ones that we've disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So next matter, next motion to be dealt with is an urgent motion for immediate disclosure from the Defence. We have the response from the Prosecution, and also -- and in addition to that, we have a reply from the Defence as well. Certain matters have already been attended to. Can I confirm that the Defence received all the materials in relation to military expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As with many responses, there will be a yes and a caveat. The material that was requested at the 65 ter conference was duly provided in two editions. We were provided with two documents, less a particular annex, and we were not provided with a third document, being a synopsis. In due course, the annex and the synopsis have both been provided. However, I should add this: That upon my personal interviewing the witness concerned yesterday, it came to my attention then that two further expertises had been prepared by him and provided to the Prosecution. The witness, understandably, did not wish to provide them directly to me, so he undertook to give them to -- to communicate with the Prosecution, which presumably he did. We then communicated ourselves with the Prosecution and have been today provided with two further expert opinions from that particular witness, Lieutenant General Ridgway. So the answer to Your Honour's question is yes, and then again yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I clarify this? Expert was --?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Lieutenant General Ridgway, Andrew Ridgway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was assisted by another expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. Well, he was, but the point I'm putting here is that he initially, and -- prepared a report, and that was provided, as it should have been. We sought some background material to that report, and after some pre-trial skirmishing, the Prosecution ultimately agreed to provide that in the terms that Your Honour will have seen at the 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When I went to visit him, he told me for the first time that he actually prepared two other reports, additional reports. They have been provided to us, after our request, today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in light of the reply filed by the Defence, is there anything to add to your response already filed on the part of the Prosecution on this issue of the urgent motion for immediate disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I just wanted to respond on this Ridgway issue. My learned friend stated that there were expert reports, two additional expert reports, which of course there are not. We did write a letter to the Defence this morning and said that our position has always been that these were informal communications done by General Ridgway in a consultative capacity to the Prosecution and were not discloseable under Rule 70(A). And we were, in the interests of transparency and good order, providing it to them now since they asked for it. We were trying to be extremely open with the Defence in this regard and giving them what they requested. But they were certainly not additional expert opinions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is put on record. And is there anything to add to make any comment to the motion requesting the OTP to provide and identify materials in relation to violations of international humanitarian laws of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have nothing to add. I think our response says it all. We have responded to all the issues raised by the Prosecution. And at this time, in respect of this, I will not say anything. But there is one other matter in respect of disclosure I would like to bring before Your Honours, and that is, this afternoon I asked Mr. Morrissey whether he would be prepared to accept and waive our requirement that we seek leave from the Chamber to disclose one further statement which has come to light today which we took November 15th of last year. It's a suspect interview of one of our current witnesses. We have the tape, but we do not have the transcript as yet. We are required by an order of the Chamber to seek leave of the Chamber to disclose anything under 66(A)(i), and Mr. Morrissey had indicated to me at the 65 ter conference that if we were to ask them beforehand, they could waive the requirement, but Mr. Morrissey says that we would have to seek leave of the Chamber, which we will do tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Chana, did you say that 66(A)(i)?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry. (A)(ii), Your Honour. I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can I hear the Defence position again.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honour. I think there would be a few clarifications to be made about that issue which came to our attention shortly before the Status Conference. The first one, to say the least, is that we are surprised to hear about this new document, considering the fact that we've been told on many repeated occasions that disclosure was finished in this case, and we heard that for the last time on Friday last week, so it's difficult for us to understand what has happened in that case. The second thing which we would like to ask the Prosecution to provide us is the date at which this interview, because it appears to be an interview, was taken, and the reason why it hasn't been disclosed to us as of yet. The third matter which would require I think an explanation on the part of the Prosecution is the status of that particular witness, Your Honour, and whether that witness is now being regarded as a suspect in that case. The last question, finally, is quite an important one for us at this stage, to be able to prepare adequately for the trial, is an indication on the part of the Prosecution as to whether this particular Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond witness will be called at trial. As was expressed during the Rule 65 ter conference and on previous occasions, the Defence has been preparing for many witnesses, spending much resources, wasting much time to prepare witnesses which are not to be called. We are quite concerned that this could be the case with that witness and other witnesses in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, this was -- this witness was among the list which exists already?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is one of the witnesses on our list. The interview, Your Honour, was taken on 15th November in another case altogether, not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A year ago?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No. This November gone, 2004, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Just before the Christmas break. And we have got the tape, of course, but we do not have the transcript. And that's why I was volunteering to give the -- hand over the tape in enough time, and when we have the transcript available, we'll be able to give that. But we can also seek leave now before Your Honours to tender this, subject to our obligations under the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chana. Apart from the general opposition against the manner of the investigation is being conducted, I don't think Defence is opposed to receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: With one caveat, Your Honour, no, we are not objecting to receiving that material, but the statement from the Prosecution as to the status of that individual as a suspect, unfortunately confirms a number of matters which we've been raising in the past, including in our motion for urgent disclosure. There is material which has not been disclosed to us, particularly material which goes to the status as suspects of those particular individuals who are now presently on the Prosecution list, and the Defence is very, very concerned about that fact. So to your question, Your Honour, no, we do not object to this material being disclosed to us, but we would like to receive urgently the material upon which the Prosecution based its conclusion that this individual is now being regarded as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the question I was about to ask. Could you respond to this last question, whether Prosecution has anything to add to the previous answer in relation to the Defence request. The Prosecution should identify those witnesses with some criminal records in relation to international humanitarian laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, all the Prosecution will say is that this particular interview was taken under a suspect interview, and when we do seek leave to admit this material, we would be giving further explanations as to the status of this particular individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was the Prosecution's response filed in relation to this urgent motion for immediate disclosure? I think it is 22nd of December last year. At that time, I think, in the least, the Prosecution should be able to say, in relation to this witness, this has -- this witness has a record of some international humanitarian law violations. But you didn't do that. That's the point the Defence wishes to raise at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We did file on December 22nd, and I think it has been an oversight, because at that time, being the Christmas break, most of the counsel who had been on the case were on leave and I think it was Mr. David Re who filed that, and perhaps it had not been brought to his attention that there was this one outstanding matter. So for that, we do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chana. And you are saying that you were not filed the written motion for this leave?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We would be very happy to file the written motion for this leave, but unless you dispense with it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do so. We don't have the name. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: One last point, Your Honour, if you allow me. We've just heard that this situation was due to an oversight. We're quite concerned that there are a number of other oversights in this case, including in relation to the status of Prosecution witnesses. This is a matter that we've been raising for a month, if not for a year or so. We would not like to be in a position of having to conduct the investigation for the Prosecution. We would like an undertaking on the part of the Prosecution that no other witness on this case is being regarded as a suspect by the Prosecution, that there is no postponement of further interviews of individuals as suspects in that case, and that every material going to the suspect status of an individual or any other material which would tend to indicate any involvement in serious violations of humanitarian laws has now been disclosed and has been identified as such to the Defence. We are very concerned that some of that material has not been disclosed to us, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In this matter, it has yet been decided as well whether to issue an order by this Trial Chamber. We'll consider this matter, bearing the submissions of today. The final motion seems to be the -- is related to pre-trial brief, supplementary explanations from the Prosecution. But this may be the one which is likely to be dealt with by this Trial Chamber, because it is related to pre-trial matters. But first of all, as Defence raised, what would be the nature and effect of that document, and what -- under what Article and Rules is the Prosecution filing this document? What is the supplementary explanation? If you could clarify on that, first of all, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have -- we filed the supplementary explanation to the pre-trial brief. As we had reviewed our Prosecution list, witness list, and our exhibit list, and since we had made quite a number of changes, we thought it would be something which we could get no notice to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber as to what the Prosecution theory is and to -- by way of explaining, the extent to which the Prosecution theory has changed or not changed, and this is just exactly what it says. It's an explanation to the pre-trial brief, with an addition. So it would be under the Rule of the pre-trial brief, Your Honour, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be a slight change of a Prosecution's assertion in terms of some factual situation. Is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there has been any particular change in the Prosecution's assertions. The theory of the case remains the same. It's 7(3) responsibility for failure to prevent and punish. I'm sorry, Your Honour; I have a bit of a cold. It is redefining the theory. Since there has been great changes on our witness list, we have reduced our witness list by two-thirds and we just thought that, to make it quite clear to the Defence as to exactly what our Prosecution theory is and to give them advance notice, it would be something valuable for them to have. It's just exactly that. It's just the advance notice to the Defence. And it's only in relation to Grabovica. We haven't done anything in relation to Ostoja, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chana. The Chamber will consider the matter in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Just in relation to that, I understand that you will consider it, Your Honour, would you just hear me briefly on it. We would invite you to regard it as being a new indictment and we draw your attention to what we say are significant new facts that are raised in it, asserted in it. And without being exhaustive about it, you could have regard to the assertion that the inspection team and the RKM, which it had attached to had become an operations group, to the timing of notice for Mr. Halilovic, a fundamental matter, which is now expressed to be on the 8th or the 9th, there are numerous other matters of relevance. But whilst we are grateful to my friend for the indication that she gave, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond we do not regard it as simply a helpful explanation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. I think somewhere in the process, the Prosecution alluded the possibility of a future -- another amendment of the indictment. Could you clarify on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. We had in that particular motion said that we will be asking for an amendment in respect of one other matter, and that is the date, Your Honour, which was the 8th and the 9th. At the moment we have only asserted the 9th and we would like to amend the indictment to state 8th and 9th. That is the full extent of the amendment that the Prosecution had foreshadowed in this motion that we might bring before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it the Prosecution position that the Trial Chamber at the later stage, at the judgement stage, cannot decide otherwise unless there's a change, amendment of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour. The Trial Chamber of course would be at liberty to decide that, depending how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm referring to whether, for example, it is 8th or 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, of course, at the end of the case, the Trial Chamber would be quite within its rights to see what the evidence states and amend it accordingly, but this was something that we had put forward and since we are still seeking certification and we are awaiting the ruling on that particular amendment, we will wait for that before we move on this other amendment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My query is that if, as you put it just now, if the Trial Chamber is free to decide on the date of notification, which is a bit different from the passage written in the indictment, why do you bother to amend it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, that's quite correct, Your Honour, and we thought for good order we might do so. And now that we see that the Defence pre-trial brief, Your Honour, that -- whether it will be the 8th or the 9th or the 10th, or for all three days, they have alleged that their client was not in the particular location. So I do not think in that event it will prejudice the accused greatly. So if they were alleging that their client was not on that two days but not the third, then perhaps it would have prejudiced the accused, but now that we have seen the Defence pre-trial brief it doesn't make any difference because their position appears to be that for all three days their client was not in Grabovica. So to that extent, perhaps it would not be necessary at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Chana. We will bear all the submissions in mind in deciding this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. But may I take the liberty to add to it very briefly that this matter of notice is important. We need to be told straight away. We have to prepare this case. It's only two weeks away. The Prosecution should now undertake to move that motion, if they're going to do so, or abjure to do so. Because we're being kept hanging in relation to it. So we call upon, to the extent that we can do in this court now, we call on the Prosecutor to indicate that they will file that motion straight away. Because it has nothing to do whatsoever with the Uzdol motion or the certification. It can be done now. It's simply a matter for the Prosecutor to do it, and we submit they should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Defence is not opposed to the amendment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The Defence is opposed to the amendment. We need to know whether we're filing it, or whether they're persisting with it. We certainly do not accept the gloss that's been placed on the pre-trial brief of the Defence filed long ago in response to what we say is quite a different case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that. Is there any difficulty on the part of the Prosecution to file the motion to amend the indictment right now, as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There's no difficulty at all, and we could, but we are very much guided by what Your Honours told us today, is that perhaps it might not be necessary after all, and especially since, as I said, after seeing the Defence pre-trial brief, no prejudice would be caused to the accused. And in relation to what my learned friend said, I would like to state that they were given an opportunity to amend their pre-trial brief, like the Prosecution did, but they have said that their pre-trial brief stands even though it was written about a year ago or so ago. So we can just take it from that that whatever they assert in the pre-trial brief is true today. And in that pre-trial brief, for all three days, which is the 8th and the 9th and the 10th, Your Honour, they assert that the accused was not in Grabovica. So if there was any question of alibi, Your Honour, and the date was very crucial to that, of course we would have moved to amend, but as Your Honour stated earlier on, perhaps it would not be necessary, since after the case is heard and the evidence will show which particular date it was, and -- so at this point, all I will say is we will take it under advisement and see whether we'll still need to move the Court and amend the indictment. And if we do, it will be done very shortly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. Defence is entitled to understand the nature of the case and whether, apart from the theoretical approach, if you intend to amend the indictment, could you do that in a week's time from today?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is so ordered. So let me be clear about the number of witnesses in the trial. If you could clarify on this. What's the number of live witnesses, as it stands now, and how would it be changed if the motion would be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment, there are 37 live witnesses, one expert, and eight 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the case if the motion would be admitted, motion to vary the number of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the motion says in our confidential annex, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the number of eight 92 bis witnesses are eight, and two among which the Defence is not opposed to the admission of the statements without cross-examination. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Your Honour. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Agreed facts. I understand that the both parties said to commit themselves to make some further progress. Can I expect both parties to make -- file submissions how far they can agree with the briefs, pre-trial briefs submitted by the other party, for example, so whether they can indicate as far as they can agree to the assertion of the other party by the time of the Pre-Trial Conference which is to be held by the Trial Chamber. I think that can assist the Trial Chamber in one way or another. But yes, can I hear from Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the Court is entitled to call for that. It clearly would assist the new Chamber that's coming. We would like to cooperate. We are in real difficulties because of what we say is the shifting sands of this Prosecution. We say there are changes to the indictment, to the pre-trial brief, there are changes that have come and changes that are coming and we still don't know what they are. The exhibit list, which has been foreshadowed to be amended, has not been provided to us yet. New exhibits are said to be in preparation to be provided. We haven't been provided with those yet. We don't know whether they're old exhibits that have assumed a new significance or whether they are now exhibits altogether that may attach some or all or none to the witnesses sought to be added. And for those witnesses, committing to an agreement to any part of the Prosecution's current array of pre-trial material is risky and uncertain. We wish to do it, and we commit to do it, but in the current state of uncertainty, we feel afraid to do it, because we're exposing ourselves to what we see as shifting, uncertain facts and assertions of facts. We have endeavoured to engage in a dialogue with the Prosecution already, and have met with some discussions, but as things currently stand, restricting the question of our pre-trial discovery -- sorry - of agreement of facts to the pre-trial briefs, as Your Honour did, we're not in a position to agree, as things currently stand, until we have some more certainty about the way the case is being put. We don't do so to be obstructive but we do so because, frankly, of a fear of the shifting sands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That having been said, I would expect both parties make their best efforts to produce some agreed facts, and I would expect the both parties to file, in writing, before the Trial Chamber, before the Pre-Trial Conference, a written submission which states the range of facts they can agree, as far as they can. For example, I have no doubt that Defence can agree with the age of Mr. Halilovic. For example, that's a very simple thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be no difficulty with any such factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or any factual explanation in the indictment; names of victims, number of victims, whether they were killed or not. There will be a number of facts --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour -- THE COURT: -- that Defence can consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- we will. Although, Your Honour, it has to be said, Your Honour has identified some areas where there may well be legitimate controversy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Also background facts, historical background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I should indicate to Your Honour that we're in current live and not preliminary discussions with the Prosecution about that. We've urged the adoption of certain facts from indictments brought by the Prosecution already in relation to background facts. Some discussion took place at the 65 ter conference that Your Honour noticed. We hope the Prosecution will agree to many of the facts which they themselves have alleged in other prosecutions which we say are legitimate facts, easy to agree upon, not in scandal or in conflict with any other decisions that may come in the future. We'll persist with that. We think those facts should, of course, be admitted and that's what we mean to do. The uncontroversial facts that Your Honour referred to, of course we will persist with, but the crunch comes and the crisis comes, of course, with facts that are alleged in the pre-trial brief and, Your Honour will appreciate, simply on the material which you've seen today, perhaps what the fears of the Defence are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I come back to the exhibit list. When is the Prosecution able to finalise its position on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We stated at the 65 ter, Your Honour, that we will be in a position to file our exhibit list on 14th of January, which is Friday. We don't intend to add many exhibits, Your Honour, and these are exhibits which we have collected in recent times, so it's not something that we had in-house already. And I do not want to put -- commit myself to a figure, but they're not going to be more than about 25 exhibits, Your Honour, which we will be adding to the exhibit list from new collections. So the Defence need not be too concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: -- about the new exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I make no hostile comment because we don't know what we're getting, Your Honour. The comment that we make is, and it's one that, Your Honour, when you come to consider, ask the crucial question, are we ready for trial, we are doing our best to be ready for trial and this is what we're against. We're going to receive new material and we're going to be preparing at the pace dictated by the Prosecution. We have plenty to do ourselves in preparing for this case and it's very regrettable that we find ourselves in this position. Having said that, we must simply await developments and await the Prosecutor when it sees fit to give us that material. But of course, when it comes, we reserve our position to object to it being added and to deal with it appropriately in motions. At this stage, it's simple hollow words because we don't know what we're getting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that. Could you shorten the period? Could it be done in a week's time from today, until the Wednesday next week? No, no, no. I beg your pardon. 14th is Friday of this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Friday, Your Honour. If you want to give us more time, until next Wednesday, Your Honour, we would be very pleased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was mistaken. Then it is so ordered. I think I dealt with all the items I planned to raise. Then I -- can I hear from the parties, anything which it likes to raise. Can I hear from the Prosecution. Is there anything to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing else to raise at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We hope it doesn't seem disrespectful to say that we understand that the Chamber is dedicating all of its attention in the best way that it can to these matters and we're grateful for that, because the sooner we have those rulings, the sooner we can plot our course and in particular deal with agreed facts, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I expected that you -- to raise something in relation to the return date of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Pardon me. I'll deal with that now, if it's appropriate. Yes. In relation to that matter, it's currently -- the current state of affairs is that he's required to return here and present himself, according to the usual arrangements, on the 17th. Your Honour will be familiar with the feast of Bajram, B-a-j-r-a-m, which is to be celebrated. Mr. Halilovic is a person with a family, and he has instructed us that he is very keen and desirous of spending that precious time with his family, if possible. Our motion -- Your Honour will also be aware that there's a motion before the President for accommodation or alternate accommodation arrangements to be made. Now, it's our submission and it's raised live in court now rather than by motion, for a good reason, that he be permitted to return on the 21st of this month, to enable him to spend that time in that religious festival with his family. It's an unusual request, but in the circumstances, his position is unusual. And the reason why that is is because he's been effectively on provisional release for a long time. As we understand it, there's no complaint made about his conduct while on provisional release. He seems to have conducted himself in a way which would give the Tribunal confidence that he'll attend. He's fulfilled his obligations. We submit you could deal with it safely on that basis, that he'll answer his obligations. We understand that although it does impose some burden upon the Tribunal to bring individuals back in the way that they have to, in fact, in this instance, it would only require the deployment of one person. It does require some administrative work to be performed, but it won't require major difficulties. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down for the benefit of the booths, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, you are being asked to slow down for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey will now slow down. It's effectively a bail application and I speed up for that reason, Your Honour. Because of his record, because of the religious festival, because he's been on provisional release, we request that his liberty be extended to the period -- to the date of the 21st, and that unless there be some reason by way of misbehaviour or something of that nature, that he be permitted to come back under supervision on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. First of all, I would prefer the motion to be filed in writing so that the Chamber can consider more conveniently. And though informally I was informed by the relevant authority that 21st is not practicable, given that that day is a UN holiday, and the Chamber will consider the matter in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We shall undertake to file the motion, and the explanation for not doing it in writing is because it triggers the usual elapse of days which potentially took us outside or beyond the period which we sought. Now that we've raised it at a live time, as we have done, we will comply with your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey. Is there anything you'd like to raise at this moment? Having no further things, then -- let me check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In relation to the accused's return date, does the OTP have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the OTP's position really, I would leave the matter to the Court. I think it is a matter of logistics. As we heard at 65, it's very, very difficult. As long as we have him on the 24th in the dock, I think that's all we are concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will not wait for the Prosecution's response for the filing of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having said that, the hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: at 3.53 p.m.
